The basal metabolic rate of Gerbillus perpallidus has been measured at 48.2 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 48.2 milliliters of oxygen per hour] under a body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], a value consistent with the modest energetic demands expected of a small desert rodent. Neonates of this species emerge weighing just 2.24 grams [Wwb = 2.24 grams], a remarkably low birth mass that reflects the altricial state typical of murid rodents. Female Pale gerbils ultimately attain an adult body mass of 50 grams [Wwi = 50 grams], a size that places them among the smaller representatives of the genus Gerbillus. This substantial increase from birth to adulthood underscores the rapid post-natal growth trajectory that characterizes this species, an adaptation likely linked to the ephemeral productivity pulses of its Saharan habitat. The contrast between the minute neonates and the full-grown females is striking and typical of desert-adapted small mammals.

Under controlled thermal conditions maintained at 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C], females produce litters of approximately 4.5 pups per litter [N_R_i = approximately 4.5 pups per litter] and can complete up to three litters annually [F_R_i = up to three litters annually], a reproductive schedule that allows for considerable population turnover in favorable years. Gestation proceeds rapidly, with a gestation period of 20 days [tg = 20 days] when measured at an ambient temperature of 35.3 °C [T = 35.3 °C], representing a short intrauterine development phase that is characteristic of small-bodied gerbillines. The newborn pups are entirely dependent on maternal care during the initial weeks of life. Suckling juveniles progress through a relatively compressed developmental sequence before reaching nutritional independence. The timing of parturition is tightly linked to resource availability in the wild.

The weaning period concludes at 20 days after birth [tx = 20 days after birth] under the same thermal conditions of 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C], marking the transition to independent feeding on seeds and green plant matter. This abbreviated dependency period is a common life-history strategy among desert rodents, enabling mothers to rapidly initiate subsequent litters. Following weaning, the juvenile animals must quickly develop the physiological and behavioral capacities necessary for survival in an arid environment. Post-weaning mortality rates are likely high, a pattern observed in many small mammal species inhabiting unpredictable habitats. The combination of a short gestation and an equally brief nursing interval allows the Pale gerbil to compress its reproductive cycle, potentially producing several cohorts during a single favorable season. This life-history strategy appears well suited to the desert environment.

Puberty, defined as the attainment of sexual maturity, occurs at approximately 93 days after birth [tp = approximately 93 days after birth] when individuals are maintained at 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C], a value that suggests a relatively fast developmental schedule compared to some other members of the Muridae. This relatively short interval from birth to reproductive capability allows the Pale gerbil to achieve rapid population growth under favorable environmental conditions. Females reaching this threshold can begin contributing to the next generation within just over three months of their own birth. The swift maturation stands in contrast to the more prolonged developmental schedules observed in some temperate gerbil species, reflecting the selective pressures of an arid environment where reproductive opportunities may be temporally constrained. Early maturation is a classic correlate of high population turnover in small desert mammals, and the Pale gerbil exemplifies this pattern.

Maximum longevity in the Pale gerbil has been estimated at approximately 5.5 years [am = approximately 5.5 years] under captive conditions maintained at 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C], a lifespan that is comparatively extended for a rodent of its modest body size. This combination of rapid early development, high reproductive output, and relatively long adult survival describes a life-history strategy that is somewhat unusual among small murids. The species appears to balance early and frequent reproduction with a sustained adult life span, a pattern perhaps linked to the unpredictability of desert resource pulses that may favor iteroparous individuals capable of multiple breeding attempts across several seasons. Long-term field studies would be valuable to confirm whether wild populations approach this captive longevity estimate or experience elevated mortality from predation and environmental extremes. The gerbil's physiological adaptations to heat and aridity likely contribute to its extended survival. Within the genus Gerbillus, species such as G. gerbillus from coastal dune systems exhibit shorter lifespans, highlighting the variation in longevity across similar-sized congeners.
